headline: SW Ledge Slack at 6:52: Bass Holding Deep, Bonito Knocking on Block Island's Door
subhead: Full moon current is stacking bait on the Ledge and pushing the first bonito scouts toward Rhode Island water — here's where to be when they arrive.
body_markdown:
Slack water at SW Ledge hit 6:52 this morning. I had the boat parked over 55 feet, right on the eastern edge where the ledge drops into the channel, and for about eighteen minutes the current went dead flat before the flood started building out of the south. That window is everything right now. With this full moon pushing exaggerated tidal current all week, the difference between fishing the Ledge at slack versus fishing it twenty minutes into the flood is the difference between marking bait and marking nothing.

Striped bass are still here, but they've gone strictly low-light on me, same as everywhere south of the Cape this time of year. The water up top is warm enough that daytime fishing over the Ledge is mostly a formality — I'm marking fish deep, hugging the structure, refusing to come up and chase anything until the sun drops or the current really starts ripping. My best bass this week came at last light and into full dark, working the down-current side of the Ledge with big Savage Gear sand eels and 2-ounce bucktails dressed with white pork rind, bounced slow along bottom in 45 to 60 feet as the tide turned to flood. Two fish over 30 pounds came off that drift Tuesday night, both in the same fifteen-minute stretch right as the current hit its peak push. That's the pattern — find the peak of the tide, not the beginning or the end, and be ready when it happens.

Now the bonito. We flagged this ten days ago — said the sequence would run RI breachways and the Vineyard rips first, then Block and Montauk behind that within the week. That's exactly how it's playing out. The Race and Fishers Island Sound are seeing real bonito now, and Vineyard boats are reporting fish on the south side. Nothing confirmed yet right off Sandy Point or North Light, but every year the pattern is the same — those fish work west and south along the warm edge until they hit the rip lines off the Block, and with surface temps holding in that favorable low-to-mid 70s band, I don't think we're more than a few days out. I've got small Deadly Dick and Deceiver patterns rigged and ready on 20-pound fluoro leader, because when they show at Sandy Point or the rip off North Light, it happens fast and it happens in a tight window on the tide change. I'll be running the east side of the island at first light starting this weekend, watching for diving terns and nervous water. If you're headed out there, don't wait for someone else to confirm it — the first wave always comes and goes before word gets around.

Fluke fishing has been the most dependable thing going, and the full moon swing is actually helping here rather than hurting. Doormats are sitting on the channel edges off Block Island — the drop-off south of the harbor entrance and the deeper water off Charlestown Breachway corridor — where the current stays cooler and keeps bait pinned against structure. I'm dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, on the last two hours of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming when the drift speed is manageable. Landed a 7-pounder Wednesday in 38 feet drifting the edge of the Ledge itself, right where the sand gives way to rock — that transition line is holding fish all week.

Sea bass remain steady out on the reef structure south of the island, particularly the rockier stretches off Clay Head where the bottom breaks up hard. They're sitting right around the thermocline, same as they have all summer, so I'm fishing high-low rigs with squid strips and Gulp, working depths from 50 to 70 feet. Nothing spectacular, but a consistent fifteen-to-twenty keeper day if you put in the bottom time and move when the marks thin out.

Bluefish have been mostly a bait story. Snapper blues are thick in the Great Salt Pond and back in the Galilee channels, which is good news for anyone with a kid and a bobber rig. The adult blues are out there too but they're staying tight to bunker schools rather than spreading across open water — I've seen a few showers of bait get worked over off Sandy Point at dawn, gulls diving hard, blues slashing through peanut bunker for five or ten minutes before it shuts off just as fast as it started. If you see that happen, don't waste time — get a metal in there immediately.

Looking ahead, the moon's still working strong through the weekend before it eases off mid-week, so I'd fish the peak tide pushes at SW Ledge while that current stays exaggerated — it's concentrating both bait and bass right now. And I'd keep one eye on Sandy Point and the North Light rip every morning this week for those first bonito. Based on how fast they moved into the Race and the Vineyard, Block Island's turn feels close. Worth being out there when it happens rather than reading about it after.
